newsitem.title: FRANCE: UPDATED - What to expect from French audit.
newsitem.headline: UPDATED - What to expect from French audit.

text.p: An audit of public finances ordered by France's new Socialist-led government will be released on July 21. Following are updated details:
MOTIVES
The new Socialist-led government elected on June 1 ordered the audit to decide what action was needed to curb the deficit in preparation for European monetary union.
TIMING OF ANNOUNCEMENT
The audit, being carried out by two members of the Court of Auditors, Philippe Nasse and Jacques Bonnet, will be submitted to Prime Minister Lionel Jospin on Monday July 21 at 0700 GMT.
Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn will present the results of the audit, and measures planned by the government to curb the deficit at a news conference at 0830 GMT.
Nasse and Bonnet will present the audit to a closed-door hearing of the parliamentary finance committee at 0900 GMT.
Strauss-Kahn is to testify before the same committee at 1300 GMT.
WHAT TO EXPECT
1997 BUDGET
The audit will forecast the total public deficit, which comprises central government spending, welfare and local authority spending, for this year.

Government sources say the audit will show the deficit at around 3.5 to 3.6 percent of gross domestic product, compared to 3.0 percent forecast in the 1997 Finance Act. Some have suggested the figure could be nearer 3.7 percent.

The auditors are expected to give a revised figure for the central government budget deficit and welfare deficit. These were forecast in the 1997 Finance Act at 284 billion francs and 30 billion francs respectively.

To provide a complete picture of public finances, the auditors would also need to calculate the potential surplus or shortfall in national unemployment fund UNEDIC and in local authority budgets and other areas of state spending.
A leaked letter from former prime minister Alain Juppe to Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, dated June 2, gave the following details on the 1997 budget:

-- Total revenues are seen at around 35 billion francs less than expected, due to a 15 billion franc shortfall in central government revenues, mainly VAT (sales tax), a 10 billion franc shortfall in payroll taxes to finance welfare spending and the loss from the budget of a nearly 12 billion franc surplus previously expected from national unemployment fund UNEDIC.

-- Total spending needs are seen at 23 billion francs more than expected, partially offset by five billion franc savings on debt service charges and a centre-right spending freeze on 10 billion francs in credit lines. Juppe said this would leave only eight billion francs to be covered.
The new government however has since partially reversed the 10 billion franc spending freeze.
1997 WELFARE DEFICIT

The central social security accounts, which use payroll taxes to fund pensions, healthcare and family benefits, are expected to show a deficit some five billion francs more than the 30 billion francs originally expected, while there is a deficit of a further five billion in other social security accounts, Juppe said.
The government could save some money on welfare this year through a plan to limit family allowances for the higher paid.
ACCUMULATED WELFARE DEFICIT
Juppe however warned the government it needed to take action to deal with the accumulated welfare deficit in 1996 and 1997.

The previous government set up last year a welfare debt repayment fund, CADES, which is borrowing on capital markets to fund the debt and using proceeds from a new tax, the RDS, to repay it. CADES however only covered debt up to the end of 1995, plus a forecast deficit of 17 billion in 1996.

Since the 1996 deficit turned out to be 55 billion francs, the government needs to take action to deal with the remaining 38 billion franc deficit uncovered in 1996, plus a deficit of 35 billion or so this year and possibly any new deficits expected next year. The welfare system is currently being financed by temporary advances from state bank Caisse des Depots et Consignations.
1997 BUDGET REDUCTION MEASURES
Strauss-Kahn has said France will not cut the deficit as far as 3.0 percent of GDP this year, but will try to reduce the figure forecast in the audit by a few percentage points.
A reduction of 0.3 percentage points from 3.6 percent of GDP to 3.3 percent of GDP would require the government to find extra revenues or spending cuts of around 25 billion francs.
Afternoon daily Le Monde said the government's package of measures would be for around 30 billion francs.
The following measures are being considered, according to government sources:

-- A rise in company taxes. Le Monde said on Friday this was a certainty. The government would leave the basic rate of tax unchanged at 33.3 percent but increase a 10 percent surcharge on this introduced in 1995, taking the effective tax rate to nearly 40 percent from 36.6 currently. Le Monde said the rise would be for 1997 and 1998.
Sources say small businesses would be exempt. The government has pledged action to avoid damaging investment.
-- Increasing employer social security contributions for pensions, accompanied by measures to protect the low paid.
-- Cancelling promised income taxes for the higher paid. French people are due to pay a final tranche of income tax in the autumn.

-- The Socialist party suggested in its campaign it could increase wealth tax or savings taxes, for example on life assurance. Le Monde said on Friday the government had decided against this for this year.
-- Taking funds from state-owned companies. The government traditionally taps state bank Caisse des Depots et Consignations (CDC) for funds to fill budget gaps.
-- Cutting spending. Strauss-Kahn has said he is looking for spending cuts. One source said, however, that the bulk of the package would concern revenues rather than spending.
1998 BUDGET
The government may announce plans to curb the deficit further in 1998 to reduce it to three percent of GDP in order to allay European fears about the deficit overshoot this year.

Juppe in his letter warned that the trend in public deficits pointed to a figure above four percent of GDP next year but said this could be cut to three percent "after savings on budget and welfare spending, questioning some fiscal spending and tapping exceptional non-fiscal revenues."
Economic growth was not having a strong enough effect on government and welfare revenues to allow the deficit to fall spontaneously, Juppe said.
Strauss-Kahn has said that if the audit shows a deficit this year of 3.4 percent it will be easier to bring it into line next year than if it shows 3.8 percent this year.
-- Myra MacDonald Paris Newsroom +33 1 42 21 53 81
